events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Ah, Doily Manor! What a magnificent establishment. I was personally invited, you know — the Countess herself wrote to me. We're old friends. Very old friends. The oldest of friends, in fact.
events.thinking: The chandelier catches the light and something behind my navel opens — a pull toward the gold and crystal that has no words, just the hollowing-out of proximity to value, my fingers curling against my palms before I've noticed them moving. Then I angle my shoulder and the medal swings into the chandelier light and my spine reaches upward — not decided, arrived — stretching toward something above me that hasn't happened yet, a vertical pull that lives in my upper chest and has nothing to do with the gut's hunger for the gold overhead. Hartwell glances at the ribbon and his eyes hold there for half a second and warmth floods my upper chest, sudden and sharp — seen, my breathing shifts, my spine straightens another fraction into the looking. The room sorts itself into angles — Hartwell's reactions arrive on schedule and my shoulders carry a particular ease around him because there is nothing to brace against, but Clara's attention lands on details before mine does and something pulls taut across my chest, a different tension, she doesn't settle into the reading I'm drawing of the room and my fingertips fizz against each other tracking the angles between her gaze and the corridor and the guest book where Marsh is standing with that careful smile. The Brixton Boys watch without blinking and the back of my neck prickles — not the gut's pull, not the spine's reaching, something flatter, a surface awareness that my body handles without breaking stride because the words are already forming. My jaw opens and the words find their shape — the Countess, the invitation, the old friendship — each syllable arriving with a warmth that only fabrication gives, smooth, placed, the tongue knowing exactly where to put the weight, and as the lie lands I feel something different settle behind my breastbone, lower than the recognition flush, heavier, a slow heat that has nothing to do with being seen and everything to do with the distance between what I just said and what is true — the invitation was in someone else's post box, the Countess has never heard my name, and the knowing sits in my sternum like something held on the tongue, sweet, worth turning slowly, the gap widening with every polite nod and my jaw loosening into it because I want to stay inside this, want every second of their believing to hold its weight a little longer in my chest. My fingertips still fizz — the plan is already in the speaking and the speaking is the plan — my peripheral vision mapping the corridor to my left, the staircase beyond Marsh, the library door half-open in the distance, each angle assembling through my hands while the gut's hollow pull reaches toward all of it at once, the house opening before me like something I haven't had yet but already feel the shape of in my ribs.
